sources.title: Meyers-Levy: The Influence of a Brand Name’s Association Set Size and Word Frequency on Brand Memory
sources.supported_claims: Two studies: word frequency moderates the association-set-size relationship with brand-information memory.
sources.limitations: Publisher abstract retrieved in search; publisher open failed; university PDF exposed no parsed text. No detailed sample sizes or effect sizes extracted.

sources.title: Lowrey, Shrum & Dubitsky: The Relation Between Brand-name Linguistic Characteristics and Brand-name Memory
sources.publisher: Journal of Advertising; author-hosted copy linked from ljshrum.com
sources.supported_claims: 480-brand copytesting; familiarity interactions; semantic fit, wordplay, initial plosives and unusual spelling associations with memory.
sources.limitations: US women 18–65; established national brands; mixed recall/recognition measure; secondary observational data; not auditory search or sales.

sources.title: Yorkston & Menon: A Sound Idea: Phonetic Effects of Brand Names on Consumer Judgments
sources.publisher: Journal of Consumer Research; Stanford-hosted paper
sources.supported_claims: Frosh/Frish ice-cream names altered attribute judgments and evaluations; diagnosticity/timing moderated effects.
sources.limitations: Two artificial names and one category; student laboratory populations; judgment and purchase intention rather than market purchases.

sources.title: Lowrey & Shrum: Phonetic Symbolism and Brand Name Preference
sources.publisher: Journal of Consumer Research; author-hosted paper
sources.supported_claims: Two experiments show vowel preference depends on desired category attributes.
sources.limitations: Artificial paired names; preferences rather than actual sales; English sound/category mappings not universal design rules.

sources.title: Shrum et al.: Sound symbolism effects across languages: Implications for global brand names
sources.publisher: International Journal of Research in Marketing; author-hosted paper
sources.supported_claims: French-, Spanish-, Chinese-speaking English bilinguals showed category-dependent vowel preferences.
sources.limitations: French n=106, Spanish n=88, Chinese n=181; artificial names; four product categories; bilingual selected samples; no Czech validation or real brand launch outcome.

sources.title: Laham, Koval & Alter: The name-pronunciation effect: Why people like Mr. Smith more than Mr. Colquhoun
sources.publisher: Journal of Experimental Social Psychology; author university-hosted paper
sources.supported_claims: Five studies associate pronunciation ease with more positive judgments of personal names and their bearers.
sources.limitations: Personal names, not drink brands; law-firm hierarchy component observational; no beverage sales effect demonstrated.

sources.title: Keller, Heckler & Houston: The Effects of Brand Name Suggestiveness on Advertising Recall
sources.supported_claims: Benefit-suggestive television name improved congruent-benefit recall but reduced later unrelated-benefit recall.
sources.limitations: Publisher abstract accessed; laboratory advertising recall, not commercial extension performance or sales.

sources.title: Rightsizing brand names: the effects of brand name length on brand name attitude and recognition
sources.publisher: Vrije Universiteit Brussel repository; Journal of Brand Management
sources.supported_claims: 98 participants, 36 fictional car/refrigerator/smartphone brands; longer non-word names better recognized; attitude curve differs from recognition.
sources.limitations: Repository abstract only; forced-choice recognition is not unaided recall; 3528 repeated measurements are not 3528 participants; full article unavailable.

sources.title: Policy Brief 94: Rightsizing Brand Names
sources.supported_claims: Author summary challenges two-syllable rule; discusses phonemes versus syllables and divergent recognition/attitude objectives.
sources.limitations: Same underlying study as EMP008, not independent replication; prescriptive 3–4 phoneme advice exceeds what this project should generalize.

sources.title: Aaker & Keller: Consumer Evaluations of Brand Extensions
sources.supported_claims: Extension judgments depend on perceived category fit and parent-brand quality, among other factors.
sources.limitations: Publisher abstract retrieved through search; open timed out; not an isolated test of lexical breadth or RTD expansion.
